newsitem.title: USA: U.S. PROTECTS SOME PACIFIC COAST STEELHEAD SALMON.
newsitem.headline: U.S. PROTECTS SOME PACIFIC COAST STEELHEAD SALMON.

text.p: The U.S. National Marine Fisheries Service said on Monday it was protecting five populations of Pacific coast steelhead salmon under the Endangered Species Act because of their declining numbers.

The service listed steelhead populations in the Upper Columbia River in Washington state and in southern California as endangered -- meaning they are at risk of becoming extinct in the foreseeable future.
Steelhead in the Snake River Basin, encompassing parts of Idaho, Washington and Oregon, the central California coast and the south-central California coast were listed as threatened.
A "threatened" listing means the fish are likely to become endangered in the foreseeable future.
The fisheries service said the listing would become effective 60 days from now, to give states time to make changes to bring them into agreement with the new listing.
"There is no dispute that these fish are in serious trouble," Terry Garcia, acting Commerce Department assistant secretary for Oceans and Atmosphere, said in a statement.
"Our commitment to salmon and steelhead conservation is clear. We must restore these magnificent fish."
The fisheries service urged affected western states to become active participants in finding ways to manage the impact of the listing.

The fisheries service said it would defer for six months a decision on five other steelhead populations in Oregon, Washington and California because there was considerable scientific disagreement about the status of these stocks.
Fisheries service spokesman Brian Gorman said those populations were likely to receive protection too in six months' time unless states came up with a comprehensive conservation plan in the meantime.

The Endangered Species Act prohibits anyone from directly killing an endangered species or harming the species or its habitat. The act also requires all federal agencies to ensure that their activities do not jeopardize a listed species.
The fisheries service said the number of steelhead returning to spawn in southern California rivers had fallen to about 500 now from 55,000 in the past.

In letters to the governors of Washington, Idaho, Oregon and California, the fisheries service urged a state-federal partnership in developing conservation plans to aid the recovery of Pacific steelhead.

In the letters, the fisheries service cited a range of causes for steelhead decline that would have to be addressed, including timber harvest, agriculture, water diversions, hydropower operations, gravel mining, urbanization, hatchery practices and fishing.

Because there is no commercial fishing for steelhead, the most direct impact of the listing would be felt by sport fishers later this year, when rules would go into effect prohibiting intentionally catching listed steelhead, the fisheries service said.
